steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The first storm of autumn came in sideways.

Rain slashed the windows of the Lantern Room, hissing against glass that had seen more years than anyone in the village remembered. Above the roaring wind, the old Fresnel lens at Haven Point Lighthouse turned with a steady, patient grace, sending its white beam in slow, sweeping arcs across the black sea.

Elias Morrow, lighthouse keeper, wound the mechanism by hand.

The motor had died three years back—someone from the Coast Guard had come with clipboards and distant apologies, promising a repair “soon.” No one had returned. The new GPS buoys and satellite systems had made the old tower irrelevant on official charts. Technically, the lighthouse at Haven Point was decommissioned.

Elias had not received that memo. Or if he had, he’d fed it to the stove.

He was lean and stooped, with a beard the color of anchor rope and hands permanently nicked and scarred from a lifetime of salt, glass, and oil. His blue wool sweater, darned at the elbows and cuffs, carried the faint smell of kerosene that had seeped into the threads decades ago. The lamps weren’t oil-fired anymore—too dangerous, they’d told him—but the smell never really left.

As the brass key creaked in the winding drum, the lens carriage resumed its slow rotation with a soft clack of gears. The beam swept, paused, swept again, cutting channels of clarity through the rain.

Elias exhaled, his breath fogging the glass.

“Steady on,” he murmured—not to the light, but to the night itself. “None of your foolishness.”

Thunder grumbled, distant yet, like an old dog clearing its throat.

Behind him, the spiral staircase yawned into darkness, vanishing down through the tower’s stone throat toward the keeper’s quarters and, below that, the store rooms and the long-disused fog signal chamber. The tower shifted almost imperceptibly with each gust, a small, familiar sway underfoot. Newcomers found it unsettling. To Elias, it was the same as a boat’s roll: a reminder the world was not as fixed as it pretended.

He moved through his routine without thinking. Check the temperature in the lantern room. Wipe condensation from the glass that could refract the beam. Peer through the little inspection hatch at the gearing, listening for a hitch or skip that meant it needed more grease.

He’d done these things for forty-one years.

Once there had been a schedule pinned to the wall, laminated and official, outlining inspections, log entries, radio checks with the harbor master. Once, a supply boat had nudged the little dock every second Thursday, bringing boxed food, new batteries, maybe a new radio if the old one had finally died.

Now the radio was only turned on for the weather report. Most days, only static answered.

The village below had changed, too. The fish cannery that had been the heartbeat of Haven Point closed. The boats that once clogged the little harbor at dawn had dwindled to a scattering—charter vessels for tourists in summer, a handful of stubborn fishermen in worn hulls the rest of the year. The children who used to shout up at him from the breakwater, asking if they could come see the big light, had grown and left. The school had closed. The post office merged with the next town over.

Haven Point shrank around him, like a coat he kept outgrowing in reverse.

But ships still passed.

In the worst storms, when even the new beacons vanished behind walls of water, Elias would sometimes see the faint glow of a bridge’s running lights, or the stubby silhouette of a trawler crawling toward the harbor. He imagined the relief of some exhausted captain when a thin white blade of light cut through the chaos, saying: Here. Here is land. Here is warning. Here is home.

That was enough.

He finished his check and went downstairs, lamp-light flickering ahead of him as he descended. In the keeper’s kitchen—the stone-walled room that had served three generations of Morrows before him—he set the kettle on the tiny gas stove. The copper kettle clicked and pinged as it heated, steam beginning to coil up through the spout.

On the wall above the table, framed in cheap oak, hung a fading photograph. Three figures stood on the rocks by the lighthouse: a younger Elias, his wife Mae, and their daughter June, all windblown and squinting into the sun. Mae’s hand was on June’s shoulder, steady as a keel. June, barely ten, clutched a bright red kite, its tail snapping straight in the invisible wind.

June had left for the city as soon as she could. That was years ago, before the cannery died, before the lighthouse was removed from the charts. She called twice a month—Sundays without fail—if the storm didn’t knock the phone lines.

“Dad, you can’t stay there forever,” she would say.

And he would answer, as he always did, “Forever’s a long time, June. I’m only staying tonight.”

And every night was tonight.

The kettle whistled. He made tea, strong and tannic, with a splash of condensed milk. Sitting at the small wooden table, he listened to the wind trying the windows and sipped carefully, his knees humming with an old ache that flared when weather turned.

On the far side of the kitchen sat an object that didn’t belong: a cardboard box half-unpacked, its flaps open like a mouth mid-sentence. Inside, bubble wrap glinted around an LED lamp assembly, the new, efficient light the representatives from the maritime authority had delivered six months ago.

"This’ll run itself once we hook up the panel," the younger of the two had said, tapping the box. "No need for anyone to stay. We’ll get you set up with a cottage down in town, sir."

“Who maintains it?” Elias had asked.

“It doesn’t need much. Automatic. Self-contained. You can monitor it from your phone, if you like.”

Elias didn’t own a mobile phone. The signal barely made it up the cliffs anyway.

He’d signed the acknowledgment forms with a stubby pencil, then stacked the box in the kitchen corner. It sat there still, gathering a thin film of salt-damp dust.

In the Lantern Room, the old bulb burned warm and constant. He trusted it. He knew its sound: the faint hum, the barely audible flicker when the wind rattled the glass.

Automation, he’d decided, could wait a little longer.

A gust hit the tower so hard it rattled his mug on the table, jolting him back to the present. The bulb of the hanging oil lamp flickered; the flame faltered, danced, steadied.

The phone on the wall rang once, then died.

Elias froze.

The phone almost never rang except on Sundays or if the harbor master needed something. And the harbor master, these days, mostly needed nothing.

He set his tea down and went to the phone, lifting the receiver. Silence. Only the faint hiss of a dead line.

The wind moaned on.

He frowned, thumb tapping the hook switch a few times. Nothing. Probably a line down somewhere along the cliff road. It happened every few winters.

He was turning away when a distant sound filtered up through the stone: a low, muffled thump, then another. It could have been thunder. It could have been the sea battering the rocks.

It could have been something else.

Elias headed for the narrow window over the sink. From here, he could see only a slice of ocean, the black wedge between two hunched shoulders of cliff. Rain streaked the glass, making the world beyond look smeared. Far out, the lighthouse beam swept, its white rib slicing the dark.

For a moment, he saw nothing. Then something small and red winked in the distance, almost immediately swallowed by a wave.

He leaned closer, heart ticking faster.

Another flash of red. A light, there and gone. Too low to be a ship’s navigation lamp. Too irregular to be one of the new buoys.

He went back to the cupboard above the stove and pulled out the binoculars, heavy and cold in his hands. Wiping the window with his sleeve, he raised them and focused, fingers stiff.

There. Between the crests—a smear of color, then the clear, hard image of a small boat, maybe eighteen feet. A skiff, open to the weather. It appeared at the top of a wave, half sideways, then slipped into the trough, swallowed by darkness.

The red he’d seen was the weak blink of a handheld flare. Someone in the boat waved it, the movement wild and desperate. The light fizzled, spat sparks, then extinguished.

Elias lowered the binoculars. His throat had gone dry.

“Fool,” he whispered, not sure whether he meant the storm or whoever was out there.

Protocol, once, would have been clear: radio the harbor master, alert the Coast Guard station down the coast, keep the light strong and the horn sounding. But the fog horn had fallen silent years ago, its compressor broken and not replaced. The little Coast Guard post had been closed in the latest round of “consolidations.” The harbor master, Robbie, lived alone in a house above the empty marina and slept like the dead in bad weather.

Elias lifted the binoculars again. The skiff reappeared, closer now. Between flashes of lightning, he could make out two figures: one slumped, one moving.

He didn’t think. He only moved.

Upstairs to the Lantern Room first. The lamp’s glow bathed the glass and brass in a warm, steady pallor. He checked the rotation—smooth, unbroken. The storm clawed at the tower, but the beam kept its rhythm.

He grabbed the switch for the auxiliary lamp—a smaller halogen mounted below the main lens, meant for emergencies. When he flipped it, a second, narrower beam burst forth, pointed more sharply toward the harbor mouth. A stronger mark, a clearer arrow.

“Come on then,” he muttered. “See what you’re meant to see.”

Down again, past the keeper’s quarters to the ground floor, where his old foul-weather gear hung like a row of patient ghosts.

He wrestled into the heavy yellow jacket, its waxed canvas stiff with age. The matching trousers stuck at the knees but settled with a grunt and a yank. Boots next, thick rubber that came up to mid-calf. He yanked the old wool cap from its peg and jammed it over his white hair.

At the door, he paused only a heartbeat, listening to the storm’s fist on the other side.

“You be reasonable,” he told it, and stepped out.

The wind hit like a live thing, trying to shove him back into the tower. Rain slapped his face hard enough to sting. The path from the lighthouse down to the small concrete jetty was steep, cut into the cliffside—fifty-seven steps, carved and poured by his grandfather “back when men still made things,” as his father used to say.

They were slick now, dark with moss and running water.

He took them one at a time, hand wrapped around the rusted rail, boots thudding. Each breath seared cold in his lungs. His knees complained, then shouted. He didn’t slow.

At the bottom, waves clawed at the rocks, flinging white spray higher than his head. The little sheltered notch that passed for a harbor at Haven Point was mostly a suggestion in weather like this. The breakwater, a jumble of granite thrown out into the sea, took the worst of the swells, but only barely. Water surged in, churned, and tried to climb the walls.

Tied to a cleat on the inner side of the jetty, bumping and straining, was Elias’s dory.

Blue paint flaked from its sides. Its name—June’s Wish—was almost worn away. The oars lay in the bottom, lashed down with a length of rope, a tarp crumpled in the bow.

He hesitated—a flicker, a second. He was not young. The sea was not gentle. But somewhere out beyond the breakwater, a small skiff with two souls aboard was a bad roll away from capsizing.

“Self-contained,” the man with the LED had said. “Automatic.”

There was nothing automatic about this.

Elias stepped from stone to boat in the brief lull between waves, landing harder than he meant to. His knee stabbed white pain up his leg, but he stayed upright. He dropped, one hand on the gunwale, and fumbled for the mooring line.

Untied, the dory leapt forward, eager. He snatched an oar and jammed its blade against the wall, pushing off, trusting the years in his muscles more than any calculation. The dory spun, nose toward the opening in the breakwater, and the full force of the wind hit.

For a moment, he almost lost the oar. Fingers tightened, joints popping, he dug the blade back into the water and pulled.

Rowing out of the little cove was like dragging the boat through mud. Each swell tried to throw him backward, each gust pushed at his chest and shoulders. His arms burned. The dory slammed into troughs, climbed crests, sending sheets of cold spray over him, under his hood, down his neck. The lighthouse beam swept across his back, then out again, over the sea.

Lightning carved a jagged line across the sky. Thunder answered like a gunshot. For a heartbeat, the world turned silver, and he saw it: the skiff, thirty yards beyond the breakwater, broadside to the waves, one figure waving frantically.

“Hold her nose to it!” he tried to shout, but the wind tore the words away.

He dug both oars deep, ribs aching, and inched closer.

The first clear look he got at them came between waves. The one at the bow had collapsed, sprawled awkwardly, one arm over the gunwale, fingers trailing in the water. The other—young, from the look of the small, hunched shape—clung to the middle seat, one hand on the useless tiller, the other raised.

The skiff’s motor lay dead, cowling half-off, like a broken jaw.

“Here!” Elias bellowed. “Here!”

The head snapped toward him—a pale, drenched face, hair plastered to the cheeks. Eyes wide and dark. A girl. Sixteen, maybe. Seventeen at most.

Her mouth formed a word he couldn’t hear. She tried to stand; the skiff rolled. She dropped back, arms wrapping around the body in the bow.

Another wave hit them both, drenching, heavy, cold enough to numb.

He pulled, teeth gritted. The dory’s worn planks groaned but held. The lighthouse’s auxiliary beam found them again, a sword of light turning the rain into streaks of glass.

He reached the skiff on the crest of a swell that lifted both boats level. For one glorious, terrifying second, they were side by side.

“Grab the gunwale!” he shouted.

The girl let go of the unconscious figure long enough to lunge toward him, fingers closing around the slippery edge of the dory. Their boats slammed together. Wood banged wood, jarred apart, closed again.

“Rope!” he yelled. “Throw me a rope!”

Her face crumpled. She glanced wildly around the skiff’s interior. No rope. No anchor line, no spare. Only the dead motor, the red flare case, and the slack body in the bow.

He swore under his breath.

“Listen!” he roared, pouring every bit of authority he’d ever used on reluctant deckhands and headstrong young fishermen into the word. “Listen to me. Hold on to my boat. Do not let go. I’m coming over.”

Her eyes flicked once to him, then to the body at her feet.

“We’ll take him, too,” Elias said, as if there was any doubt. “But you have to hold on first.”

She nodded, jaw set tight.

He dropped one oar—the wind and current would decide for it now—and inched the boats closer with the remaining blade, short, brutal strokes that yanked at his shoulders. The next wave tried to separate them; he rode it, twisting, bringing his hull alongside hers again.

“Now!” he barked.

She shifted, lunging, both hands shooting out. Her fingers closed on his gunwale, knuckles whitening. Their little boats bucked and jostled, fighting the tether of her arms.

Elias got his own grip on the edge of the skiff. The wood was slick with rain and something thicker—blood, maybe; he couldn’t be sure.

He had not planned for how he would climb from one bucking craft to another in the middle of a storm, at his age, with one knee already an unreliable hinge. But planning, he’d long ago learned, only brought you so far.

He threw his weight.

For a breath he was over open water, nothing below him but wet air and black sea, then his boots hit the skiff’s bottom hard enough to send a stabbing shock up his legs. He stumbled, grabbed the seat to keep from going down.

The skiff lurched. The girl cried out, clutching the other boat as the distance widened, the rope of her arms stretched.

“Let go!” Elias shouted.

“Wha—”

“Let go and get in mine!”

She hesitated—the fraction of a second where fear and instinct argued—then she pushed off, vaulting, more falling than leaping, into the dory. She landed in a tangle of limbs and soaked clothes but stayed inside.

“Stay low!” he called.

He turned to the figure in the bow.

A man, older than the girl by twenty years, maybe more. Lines etched his pale face, but the rain had scrubbed away any blood or dirt. His lips were blue. His chest heaved in shallow, rapid gasps. A thick jacket was zipped up to his chin, soaked through, clinging.

“Sir,” Elias said, bending awkwardly. “Can you hear me?”

The man’s eyes fluttered open. They were the same shape, the same dark color as the girl’s. Father and daughter, then. His gaze slid from Elias to the lighthouse, then back again, unfocused.

“Came out… tried… motor…” he choked, voice shredded by cold and salt.

“Save your breath.” Elias put one arm under his shoulders. “We’re going ashore.”

The skiff chose that moment to slam broadside into a wave crest. It lurched, rocking so hard Elias felt his feet start to go. He dropped his center of gravity, squatting, hugging the man’s torso in.

The transfer, once upon a time, would have been smooth. A roll of the hips, a shove, and he’d have hauled the dead weight over himself like a sack of nets. Now his thighs screamed before he’d fully straightened, his lower back threatening to seize.

“You can do this once,” he told his body. “Once more.”
